text: Mostly because their lives go in different directions. People move to other cities, start different careers and have families, so the things that connected them at school simply disappear. It isn't always negative, though. Some childhood friendships were based only on sitting in the same classroom, and it's natural to replace them with friendships built on shared interests.

tips.kk: Lives go in different directions — сыйымды түсіндірме.
tips.ru: Lives go in different directions — ёмкое объяснение.

tips.ru: It isn't always negative, though — вторая сторона вопроса.

questions.followUp: Is it always a bad thing?
questions.question: Why do people often lose touch with their childhood friends?

text: I think they can, especially among people who share a hobby or a professional interest. I have a friend from Poland whom I met in a language-exchange app, and we've talked almost every week for two years. However, online friendships are easier to end — if someone stops replying, it just fades. Meeting in person at least once seems to make the relationship much stronger.

questions.question: Can people have real friendships online?

text: For me, reliability comes first. A good friend is someone you can call at two in the morning if something goes wrong. Honesty matters too, even when it's uncomfortable, because a friend who only agrees with you isn't much help. And I think a sense of humour is underrated — the friends I stay closest to are the ones I can laugh with.

questions.question: What qualities make someone a good friend?

text: I wouldn't say more important, but they play a different role. Family is usually there no matter what, while friends are people we choose, so they often share our interests and views more closely. For teenagers, friends can feel like the centre of the world. Later, when people have their own children, family tends to take up most of their time again.

questions.question: Are friends more important than family?

text: Generally, yes. At school or university you meet the same people every day without trying, but adults are busy with work and family, and they're often less open to new people. The best way is probably through regular activities — a sports club, a choir or volunteering — because seeing the same faces every week gives friendships time to grow naturally.
